info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 7.3: Rendering with AI: Auditing a Stylesheet You Did Not Write.

name.text: 01 Question: Today's Question: Can You Trust a Stylesheet You Did Not Write?

questiontext.text: An AI-written stylesheet runs without errors and has tidy comments. What does that tell you?

generalfeedback.text: An AI model can write a stylesheet that looks professional and runs without errors; today's job is to find out whether it carries out your decisions.

answer.text: Only that it runs; whether it carries out your decisions still has to be checked.

feedback.text: Correct. A stylesheet can run cleanly while dropping gaps, gluing words or showing the wrong layer.

answer.text: That it carries out your decision table correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Running without errors says nothing about whether the rules match your decisions.

answer.text: That it is better than the stylesheet you wrote on Wednesday.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Polish is not evidence. Only the audit can compare the two.

answer.text: That no audit is needed, because AI models do not make rendering errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Today's lesson is about the errors AI-written stylesheets commonly contain.

name.text: 02 Question: Ask for Rules, Not for a Page

questiontext.text: Why should you ask the model for a stylesheet rather than a finished page?

generalfeedback.text: Ask the model to write a stylesheet, not a page; a checked stylesheet gives the same output on every run, while every directly generated page needs a fresh audit.

answer.text: Once checked, a stylesheet gives the same output on every run, while every directly generated page needs a fresh audit.

feedback.text: Correct. The uncertainty is in the writing, which happens once; the checked rules then behave deterministically.

answer.text: A model cannot produce HTML, only XSLT.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A model can produce HTML directly; that is exactly the risky route.

answer.text: Stylesheets written by a model are always correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They need auditing too, but only once.

answer.text: A finished page would be too large to save in your repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Size is not the issue; repeatability and checkability are.

name.text: 03 Question: What Goes Wrong When a Model Renders Text Directly

questiontext.text: Which risk applies to a model rendering text directly but not to an XSLT stylesheet?

generalfeedback.text: A model rendering text directly can modernize, correct or fill in your words, while a stylesheet can only select and wrap text already in your file, so its errors are easier to find.

answer.text: It can write words that are not in your TEI, such as filling a gap with plausible text.

feedback.text: Correct. A stylesheet can select, wrap or omit your text, but it cannot invent new words.

answer.text: It can omit an element from the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A stylesheet can also omit an element, for example a gap with no template.

answer.text: It can show the wrong layer of a <choice>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A stylesheet can do that too, as the first-child rule shows.

answer.text: It can produce a page with no language declaration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both routes can leave out the lang attribute.

name.text: 04 Question: Your Three Points of Comparison

questiontext.text: The AI stylesheet and Wednesday's stylesheet disagree about how a <sic> appears. What settles the disagreement?

generalfeedback.text: Check the AI stylesheet against all three standards: the decision table for what should happen, Wednesday's output for every word, and Tuesday's page for how each mark looks.

answer.text: The decision recorded in RENDERING.md.

feedback.text: Correct. The decision table is the authority; the question is which stylesheet carries it out.

answer.text: Wednesday's stylesheet, because you wrote it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your own rules can be wrong too; the recorded decision is the standard.

answer.text: The AI stylesheet, because it is newer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Being newer gives it no authority.

answer.text: Whichever output looks better in the browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Appearance is not the test; faithfulness to the recorded decision is.

name.text: 05 Question: Writing the Prompt: What the Model Must Know

questiontext.text: How should you choose the sample of TEI lines to paste into the prompt?

generalfeedback.text: Give the model your whole decision table, a sample containing every element you use, the XSLT 1.0 and namespace requirements, your existing class names, and the page shell settings.

answer.text: By the elements they contain, so that every element in your file appears at least once.

feedback.text: Correct. An element missing from the sample is an element the model does not know exists.

answer.text: Always the first thirty lines of the body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The first lines may not contain every element you use.

answer.text: Paste the whole file, since the model needs all the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You are asking for rules, so the model needs each kind of element, not every word.

answer.text: Pick the lines with the fewest tags, so the model is not confused.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model needs to see your markup, especially the unusual parts.

name.text: 06 Question: Writing the Prompt: What the Model Must Not Do

questiontext.text: What is the main value of listing negative constraints in the prompt?

generalfeedback.text: Name every known failure in the prompt as a rule not to break; the model may still break one, but the list tells you exactly what to look for.

answer.text: If the model breaks one, you know at once what it ignored and where to look.

feedback.text: Correct. The list does not guarantee compliance, but it makes the model's choices visible.

answer.text: It guarantees the model will not make those errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A model may still break an explicit rule.

answer.text: It makes the stylesheet run faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The constraints are about correctness, not speed.

answer.text: It replaces the need for a decision table.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The constraints add to the table; they do not replace it.

name.text: 07 Question: A Complete Prompt

questiontext.text: You find you cannot write a line of the prompt explaining how <hi> should appear. What does this suggest?

generalfeedback.text: A good stylesheet prompt restates every decision and requirement from this week in plain terms; a line you cannot write points to a decision still missing from RENDERING.md.

answer.text: A decision about <hi> is still missing from RENDERING.md.

feedback.text: Correct. Every line of the prompt restates a decision; a line you cannot write points to one you have not made.

answer.text: The model will know how to display <hi>, so you can leave it out.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would let the model make the decision for you.

answer.text: <hi> cannot be rendered with XSLT 1.0.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <hi> is easy to render; the difficulty is the missing decision.

answer.text: The prompt is already too long and should be shortened.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A long prompt is expected; the gap is in your decisions.

name.text: 08 Question: Running the Model and Saving Its Answer

questiontext.text: Why commit the AI stylesheet before you change anything in it?

generalfeedback.text: Save the prompt, save the stylesheet under a new name, and commit both unedited before you change anything, so the record shows exactly what the model wrote.

answer.text: So the record shows exactly what the model wrote, before your audit changed it.

feedback.text: Correct. The unedited baseline is the stylesheet your audit applies to, and the same prompt may give a different answer later.

answer.text: Because Git cannot track later changes to an AI-written file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks every change; the point is to keep the original as a baseline.

answer.text: So that it overwrites your own reading.xsl.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Save it under a new name; your own stylesheet is one of your standards.

answer.text: Because the model's file will be deleted if not committed at once.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing deletes it; the commit is for provenance.

name.text: 09 Question: First Check: Does It Run?

questiontext.text: The AI stylesheet runs without error, but the page body is empty. The stylesheet begins with version 2.0 and xpath-default-namespace. What is happening?

generalfeedback.text: An error usually points to an XSLT 2.0 feature, and an empty page to a missing tei: prefix; a full page proves only that the stylesheet runs, not that it is right.

answer.text: lxml supports only XSLT 1.0 and ignores that setting, so no unprefixed match finds your TEI elements.

feedback.text: Correct. This is the namespace pitfall in a new form; the fix is the tei: prefix in every match.

answer.text: Your TEI file has no body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The same file renders with Wednesday's stylesheet.

answer.text: The CSS file is hiding the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The HTML itself is empty; CSS cannot be the cause.

answer.text: lxml stops with an error whenever it meets XSLT 2.0.

feedback.text: Incorrect. With this setting it gives no warning at all, which is what makes it hard to spot.

name.text: 10 Question: Second Check: Read It Template by Template

questiontext.text: In your template inventory, a template in the AI stylesheet matches no row of your decision table. What should you do?

generalfeedback.text: Pair every decision with a template and every template with a decision; a decision with no template, or a template with no decision, is where problems hide.

answer.text: Look closely: it is either something the model added on its own or a sign that your table is missing a decision.

feedback.text: Correct. Orphan templates are where problems hide, in either the stylesheet or the table.

answer.text: Ignore it, since extra templates cannot hurt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The whitespace rule in the sample is an extra template, and it glues words together.

answer.text: Delete it without reading it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It might be a genuine improvement, or reveal a missing decision.

answer.text: Copy it into your own stylesheet straight away.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing enters your stylesheet without a decision in RENDERING.md first.

name.text: 11 Question: A Sample AI Stylesheet

questiontext.text: What does the sample AI stylesheet show about plausible code?

generalfeedback.text: A stylesheet can use the namespace correctly, select only the body and carry tidy comments while still producing a page that changes, glues together and loses your text.

answer.text: It uses the namespace correctly and has tidy comments, yet its output changes, glues together and loses the text.

feedback.text: Correct. Looking well organized is no evidence of correct output.

answer.text: It fails to run because of a namespace error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It uses the tei: prefix correctly and runs.

answer.text: It produces exactly the same paragraph as Wednesday's stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its paragraph has glued words, the wrong layer and no visible gap.

answer.text: It was copied from a particular model's answer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is illustrative, written for the lesson to collect common problems.

name.text: 12 Question: The First Child Is Not Always the Right One

questiontext.text: Why is select="*[1]" in a <choice> template an error, even when its comment says it shows the edited form?

generalfeedback.text: A rule that picks the first child of <choice> depends on the order of your markup, not on your decision; select each layer by name, whatever its comment says.

answer.text: It picks whichever child comes first, so the layer shown depends on the order of your markup, not on your decision.

feedback.text: Correct. Select each layer by name, such as tei:reg|tei:expan|tei:corr.

answer.text: TEI forbids more than one child inside <choice>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <choice> always holds alternatives.

answer.text: XSLT 1.0 does not support numbered selections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. *[1] works; it just selects by position.

answer.text: The first child of <choice> is always <reg>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI Guidelines do not fix the order of the children.

name.text: 13 Question: Cleaning Up Whitespace Glues Words Together

questiontext.text: What happens when normalize-space() is applied to every text node in a TEI paragraph?

generalfeedback.text: Applying normalize-space() to all text deletes the spaces beside every element and glues words together; in mixed content, trim whitespace only where a specific rule requires it.

answer.text: The spaces at the edges of text nodes are removed, so words beside elements are glued together.

feedback.text: Correct. In mixed content, the space between words often sits at the edge of a text node.

answer.text: Only double spaces are reduced, so nothing visible changes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It also trims leading and trailing spaces, which separate words from elements.

answer.text: The stylesheet stops with an error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It runs cleanly, which is why the damage is easy to miss.

answer.text: Split words at line breaks are joined correctly everywhere.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It changes every text node, not just those before a break=no line break.

name.text: 14 Question: The Silent Gap

questiontext.text: Why are brackets added with CSS ::before not an adequate fix for an empty gap span?

generalfeedback.text: A gap template that writes an empty span, or brackets added only by CSS, hides the loss from readers and from copied text; brackets and gap details must be real text in the HTML.

answer.text: Generated content is not part of the page's text, so it is lost when a reader copies the sentence and cannot be found by search.

feedback.text: Correct. Brackets and gap details must be real text in the HTML.

answer.text: Browsers never display ::before content.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They display it on screen; the problem is that it is not part of the text.

answer.text: CSS cannot be used with XSLT output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The XSLT output links CSS files.

answer.text: The brackets would appear twice.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They appear once on screen; they are just not real text.

name.text: 15 Question: Line Breaks That Swallow Spaces

questiontext.text: You change the AI stylesheet's empty <lb/> template to write a space, but add nothing else. What new error appears?

generalfeedback.text: A line-break rule that writes nothing joins the last word of each line to the first word of the next; write a space for ordinary breaks and nothing for break=no, and test both together.

answer.text: Words split across lines with break=no now show a space inside them, such as Pro- vince.

feedback.text: Correct. Fix the ordinary line-break rule and the break=no rule together, and test both.

answer.text: Every line now begins on a new paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A space does not start a new paragraph.

answer.text: The gaps disappear from the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The line-break rule does not affect the gap template.

answer.text: No new error; the fix is complete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Without a separate break=no rule, split words gain a space.

name.text: 16 Question: The Catch-All Template

questiontext.text: Why remove a template with match="*" that simply applies templates to its content?

generalfeedback.text: A catch-all template behaves like the built-in rules but makes every undecided element look deliberate; remove it, so that elements without a rule stay visible as open questions.

answer.text: It makes every undecided element look deliberate, hiding open questions in your rendering.

feedback.text: Correct. An element without a rule should stay visible as a question you have not answered.

answer.text: It overrides all your specific templates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT prefers more specific matches, so it catches only elements without a template.

answer.text: It causes the stylesheet to crash.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It runs without error.

answer.text: It deletes the text of every element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It keeps the text; it hides the fact that no decision was made.

name.text: 17 Question: What Is Missing from the Page Shell

questiontext.text: The AI stylesheet writes <em> for supplied letters instead of Tuesday's class ex. Why does this matter if the italics look the same?

generalfeedback.text: Check the AI page shell for lang and meta charset, and check that it uses your existing class names; their absence causes no errors, only quiet failures.

answer.text: Any CSS rule written for the class ex, in reading.css or the print stylesheet, silently stops applying.

feedback.text: Correct. Class names are a contract between your HTML and your CSS.

answer.text: <em> is not valid HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <em> is valid; it just breaks the class contract.

answer.text: Screen readers cannot read <em>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is not the problem the lesson identifies.

answer.text: It does not matter at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your CSS expects .ex, so rules for that class stop working.

name.text: 18 Question: Third Check: Compare the Output Word by Word

questiontext.text: compare.py reports Words: 17 and 5 for Wednesday's page and the AI page. What does this most likely show?

generalfeedback.text: Compare the visible words of the AI page with Wednesday's checked page; equal word counts and no differences mean no words were lost, changed or glued together.

answer.text: Words in the AI page have been glued together or lost, so the two texts no longer match.

feedback.text: Correct. A clean result has equal word counts and no listed differences.

answer.text: The AI page is more concise and therefore better.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A rendering should not change the number of words in the text.

answer.text: Wednesday's page has duplicated words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wednesday's page is already checked; here the AI page glued words together.

answer.text: The script is broken, since word counts always match.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The difference is exactly what the script is meant to reveal.

name.text: 19 Question: Fourth Check: Count What the Reader Sees

questiontext.text: count.py reports one gap class on the AI page but zero brackets. What does this mean?

generalfeedback.text: Count each element in the TEI and each class and bracket on the page; a matching class with a missing bracket shows a mark that exists in the code but not for the reader.

answer.text: The gap exists in the HTML code, but the reader sees no mark of it.

feedback.text: Correct. This is why you count what the reader sees, not only the classes.

answer.text: The gap has been rendered correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A class with no visible brackets gives the reader nothing to see.

answer.text: Your TEI file has no gap.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The class is there because the TEI has a gap.

answer.text: The script cannot count brackets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It counts them in the visible text of the body.

name.text: 20 Question: Making Undecided Elements Visible

questiontext.text: Why does the audit template use priority="-1"?

generalfeedback.text: A low-priority audit template that outlines every unhandled element in red turns silent omissions into visible questions; resolve each one in RENDERING.md, then remove the template.

answer.text: So that every one of your real templates still wins, and only unhandled elements are outlined.

feedback.text: Correct. Without the low priority, the audit template could outrank specific rules such as tei:p.

answer.text: So that it runs before all other templates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Priority decides which template wins a match, and -1 makes it lose to your real templates.

answer.text: So that it removes unhandled elements from the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It wraps them in a red-outlined span; it does not remove them.

answer.text: Because XSLT 1.0 requires a priority on every template.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Priority is optional.

name.text: 21 Question: Auditing AI-Written CSS for CETEIcean

questiontext.text: Which rule in an AI-written CETEIcean stylesheet has the same flaw as *[1] in XSLT?

generalfeedback.text: Audit AI-written CETEIcean CSS for brackets made in CSS, layers chosen by position, misplaced line numbers and accidental display: none; every display choice must be one you recorded.

answer.text: tei-choice > :first-child

feedback.text: Correct. It selects a layer by position; hide and show layers by element name instead.

answer.text: tei-orig { display: none; }

feedback.text: Incorrect. That selects by element name, which is the correct approach.

answer.text: tei-p { display: block; }

feedback.text: Incorrect. That only puts paragraphs on their own lines.

answer.text: tei-unclear { color: grey; }

feedback.text: Incorrect. That styles an element by name.

name.text: 22 Question: Sorting What You Find: Three Kinds of Difference

questiontext.text: The audit outlines a <note> in red. Which kind of difference is this?

generalfeedback.text: Sort each difference into an AI error, an undecided decision, or a genuine improvement, and remember that some differences will reveal errors in your own stylesheet.

answer.text: An undecided decision: your table never covered the case.

feedback.text: Correct. Decide it in RENDERING.md first, then write the rule.

answer.text: An AI error: the model failed a clear decision.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There was no decision for <note> to fail.

answer.text: An improvement: the model handled it better.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A red outline means no rule handled it at all.

answer.text: Not a difference, so it can be ignored.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every red box goes into the audit log.

name.text: 23 Question: When the Model Is Right and You Were Wrong

questiontext.text: The AI stylesheet has a good rule for <hi rend="underline">, which you overlooked. What do you do first?

generalfeedback.text: When the model handles a case better than you did, record the decision in RENDERING.md first, then adopt, test and credit the rule; the idea may be the model's, but the decision is yours.

answer.text: Add a row for it to RENDERING.md, stating how it appears in each view and why.

feedback.text: Correct. Decide first, then take, test and credit the rule.

answer.text: Copy the template into your stylesheet straight away.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Without a row in the table, that is an inherited decision.

answer.text: Discard it, because only your own rules may be used.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adopting a good rule is reasonable, once the decision is yours.

answer.text: Replace your whole stylesheet with the AI version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One good rule does not make the rest of the AI stylesheet correct.

name.text: 24 Question: Fix, Adopt, or Discard

questiontext.text: Why should you not keep both reading.xsl and ai-reading.xsl as working versions after the audit?

generalfeedback.text: Fix the AI stylesheet, adopt only its improvements, or discard it; then finish with one checked stylesheet per view and rerun every check on the final version.

answer.text: A reader who finds both cannot tell which one made your published page.

feedback.text: Correct. Finish with exactly one checked stylesheet per view.

answer.text: Git cannot store two XSLT files in one folder.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git can store any number of files.

answer.text: lxml can only load one stylesheet per computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such limit.

answer.text: The AI stylesheet must always be deleted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You may fix it and adopt it; the point is to end with one version.

name.text: 25 Question: Worked Example: Auditing an AI Stylesheet for Maud Lewis's Letter

questiontext.text: In Olyvia's audit, the word comparison shows no differences, yet the greeting and signature run into the body. What found the problem?

generalfeedback.text: A word comparison can show no differences while a letter's greeting and signature run into the body; use the audit template and Tuesday's page to catch structural omissions.

answer.text: The audit template and Tuesday's page, because the problem is in structure, not in words.

feedback.text: Correct. No single check is enough; a structural omission keeps every word.

answer.text: The word comparison, on a second run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every word is present and in order, so it will report no differences.

answer.text: The HTML validator.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The page is valid; it just loses the letter's parts.

answer.text: The count of <choice> elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem has nothing to do with <choice>.

name.text: 26 Question: Worked Example: The 1752 Treaty and an Inconsistent File

questiontext.text: Why did the first-child rule look right on most of Andromeda's lines?

generalfeedback.text: A first-child rule can look right on most lines and fail on a few; counting layer classes on the page against <choice> elements in the TEI finds the exact number of failures.

answer.text: Most of her <choice> elements put <reg> first, so position happened to give the right layer.

feedback.text: Correct. The rule depended on element order, which carries no meaning and varied in her file.

answer.text: The rule was actually correct, and the six lines were transcription errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Her file was valid; the rule depended on an accident of order.

answer.text: XSLT corrects the order of children automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT processes the children as they appear.

answer.text: The reading view does not show <choice> elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It shows one layer of each <choice>.

name.text: 27 Question: Recording the AI's Contribution

questiontext.text: Where should you record the AI's contribution to your rendering rules?

generalfeedback.text: Record AI involvement in a comment in the stylesheet, a summary in RENDERING.md, and separate commits for the unedited and corrected versions.

answer.text: In a comment in the stylesheet, a summary in RENDERING.md, and separate commits for the unedited and corrected versions.

feedback.text: Correct. Together these show which rules came from a model, which were checked, and who is responsible.

answer.text: Only in the TEI header, as in Week 6.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Today the model wrote software that displays your text, so the record belongs with the software.

answer.text: Nowhere, since the stylesheet is not part of the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The stylesheet decides what readers see, so its origins must be recorded.

answer.text: Only in the final commit message.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Use all three places.

name.text: 28 Question: What This Week Has Built

questiontext.text: When you add lemmas to your TEI in Week 8, what should you do with this week's work?

generalfeedback.text: This week has produced checked views, rules and reusable checks; rerun them whenever your TEI changes, and treat the decision table as the start of your edition's editorial statement.

answer.text: Rerun the stylesheets and the checks, and add a row to RENDERING.md for each new element.

feedback.text: Correct. The scripts and the audit template work on any later version of your edition.

answer.text: Nothing, because rendering is finished.

feedback.text: Incorrect. New elements will need new decisions and rules.

answer.text: Start the rendering again from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The existing rules and checks carry forward.

answer.text: Ask the model to rewrite the whole stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Add rows and rules for the new elements, then rerun the checks.

name.text: 29 Question: Hypothetical Scenario: The Gap That Filled Itself

questiontext.text: In the scenario, which single step caused the invented words to be published?

generalfeedback.text: A model rendering text directly can fill a gap with plausible words; asking for rules instead of text, and counting gaps against brackets, protects readers from text that was never there.

answer.text: Asking a model for text instead of rules, and publishing its text without checking it against the source.

feedback.text: Correct. The transcription and encoding were both correct; the failure was in rendering.

answer.text: A transcription error in the TEI file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The scenario says the transcription was correct.

answer.text: A missing <gap/> element in the encoding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI contained the gap, with its reason and extent.

answer.text: A bug in the XSLT stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No stylesheet was used; the page was generated directly.

name.text: 30 Question: Review and Step 3 Checklist

questiontext.text: What does completing Step 3 give you?

generalfeedback.text: Completing Step 3 gives you final stylesheets you can defend rule by rule, an audit log of everything the model got wrong or right, and checks you can rerun as your edition grows.

answer.text: Final stylesheets you can defend rule by rule, an audit log, and checks you can rerun as your edition grows.

feedback.text: Correct. The three-step cycle for rendering is now complete.

answer.text: An AI-written stylesheet that replaces your own without review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every AI rule has been audited, and adopted only by decision.

answer.text: A finished Print-Ready Publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This week's work feeds the publication, which is due later.

answer.text: Permission to skip the decision table in future weeks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each new element still needs a row in RENDERING.md.
